sections.h: The second song: "You are my servant, Israel" (Isaiah 49:1–7)
sections.b: The servant speaks for himself to the far coasts: called from the womb, his mouth a sharp sword, he is named "Israel" (49:3), yet sent to bring Jacob back (49:5). Discouraged that he has worked "for nothing" (49:4), he receives a larger task: "I will give you as a light to the nations, / so that you may be my salvation / to the farthest end of the earth" (49:6). Simeon (Luke 2:32) and Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:47) apply the line to Jesus and the mission to the Gentiles. Every ancient witness has the name 'Israel'; only one medieval manuscript lacks it.

sections.h: The third song: the servant who listens and suffers (Isaiah 50:4–11)
sections.b: The servant has "a learner's tongue" and an ear God opens each morning (50:4–5). He does not turn back: "My back I gave to the floggers, / my cheeks to those who tore at my beard. / I did not cover my face / against insult and spit" (50:6). Confident that "the one who declares me in the right" is near (50:8), he sets his face like flint. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read the speaker as the prophet; the Gospels' accounts of Jesus slapped and spat on echo the Greek of 50:6, and Paul's courtroom questions in Romans 8:33–34 follow 50:8–9.

sections.h: The fourth song: high and lifted up, crushed for many (Isaiah 52:13–53:12)
sections.b: God announces that his servant "will be high and lifted up" (52:13), the words of God's own throne in 6:1. A 'we' then confesses that they despised him: "Yet it was our sicknesses that he carried" (53:4); "he was pierced for our rebellions" (53:5); "the LORD made the guilt of us all / fall on him" (53:6). Silent like a lamb, condemned, buried with the wicked, he becomes a guilt offering (53:10), yet "he will see light" (53:11, with the Qumran scrolls and the Greek) and "make the many righteous". Jewish interpreters read the song of Israel among the nations (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi) or of the Messiah (the Targum, which turns the suffering onto others); the New Testament reads it of Jesus (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25).

sections.h: From the servant to the servants (Isaiah 54:17)
sections.b: After 53 the book never again speaks of 'my servant' in the singular. Instead it speaks of "the LORD's servants" (54:17), whose "vindication comes from me", and chapters 56–66 return to them often. Many readers see the 'offspring' the servant was promised (53:10) in this community of servants who share his calling. Readers who take the servant as Israel see the faithful within Israel here; readers who take him as one person see his followers.

common: The four 'servant songs' are usually counted as 42:1–9, 49:1–13, 50:4–11 and 52:13–53:12.
Jewish interpreters since the Middle Ages have mostly read the servant of 52:13–53:12 as Israel.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that 'Israel' in 49:3 is a later addition, though every ancient witness has it.
R. N. Whybray argued that the servant of 53 does not die but is released from prison.

claude.title: A servant described before he is named
claude.body: The songs consistently describe the servant's work and fate but avoid a proper name except in 49:3, and even there the name is a title as much as an identity. One reading of this restraint is that the book means the figure to be recognized by what he does rather than by who he is, which would explain why both a people and a person have been seen in him. This is Claude's own suggestion, not a published thesis.

sections.b: Isaiah 45:1 calls Cyrus the LORD's "anointed", the only foreigner so named. God takes his right hand, opens gates before him and gives him Babylon's treasures "For the sake of Jacob my servant" (45:4), "though you did not know me" (45:4–5). He is "a bird of prey from the east" (46:11) and the one "the LORD loves" (48:14). The Cyrus Cylinder uses strikingly similar language of Marduk choosing Cyrus. Whether Isaiah named Cyrus in advance or a prophet of the 540s announced him is the book's central authorship question.

common: Cyrus allowed the Judean exiles to return and rebuild the Temple in 538 BC.
uncommon: The Epistle of Barnabas read 45:1 'to Christ my Lord' instead of 'to Cyrus'.

sections.b: Babylon's gods Bel and Nebo are carted off as freight (46:1–2), and the city, pictured as a pampered queen, must come down to the dust and grind meal like a slave (47:1–3). She boasts in God's own words, "I am, and besides me there is nothing" (47:8), and trusts her sorceries and star-watchers, but loses husband and children in one day (47:9). The call "Go out from Babylon!" (48:20) closes the section. Revelation 18 takes up the taunt for its own Babylon (Revelation 18:4, 7–8).

The title 'anointed' in 45:1 belongs to Cyrus, a ruler chosen for a task, not yet 'the Messiah'. The Targum, however, names the servant of 52:13 'my servant the Messiah', and the Talmud calls the Messiah "the leper of the house of Rabbi" from 53:4 (Sanhedrin 98b). Isaiah 55:3 promises 'the sure loyal love of David' to the people, which Acts 13:34 applies to Jesus's resurrection. Christians see the anointed king and the suffering servant joined in one person.

The servant carried "our sicknesses" and "our pains" (53:4), and "through his welts we have healing" (53:5). Matthew 8:17 applies 53:4 to Jesus's healings; 1 Peter 2:24 applies 53:5 to healing from sin. In Isaiah 'healing' often means the restoration of a sick nation (1:5–6; 6:10; 57:18–19). Pentecostal teaching finds bodily healing provided in the atonement; other churches read the promise first of forgiveness and finally of resurrection.

Isaiah 45:7 claims that the LORD forms light and darkness, peace and disaster: nothing lies outside his rule, including the rise of Cyrus and the fall of Babylon. The synagogue's morning blessing quotes it with 'all things' in place of 'evil' (Berakhot 11b). Isaiah 54:16 adds that God created both the smith who makes weapons and the destroyer, so that no weapon can succeed against Zion without his will.

Isaiah 53 uses the language of sacrifice and sin-bearing: the servant 'bore' the sin of many (53:12), the LORD 'made the guilt of us all fall on him' (53:6), and his life becomes an asham, a guilt offering (53:10; Leviticus 5:14–19). The goat of the Day of Atonement 'carries' Israel's guilt 'to a land cut off' (Leviticus 16:22); the servant is 'cut off from the land of the living' (53:8). Christian doctrines of the atonement have drawn on the chapter more than on any other Old Testament text.

"Are you not the one that hacked Rahab apart, / that ran the dragon through?" (51:9). The prophet calls on the LORD's arm to act as at the beginning, then identifies the victory with the drying of the sea at the exodus (51:10). In Babylon, where Marduk was praised for splitting the sea goddess Tiamat, the claim was pointed: Israel's God is the one who conquers the waters.

The return from Babylon is told in the words of the exodus: water from the rock (48:21), the sea dried and the deep made a road for the redeemed (51:10), the LORD going before and behind (52:12; Exodus 13:21; 14:19). But this time Israel will not leave "in a rush" (52:12; Exodus 12:11), and the trees will clap their hands (55:12).

Zion, who says "I had lost my children and was barren" (49:21), is surprised by crowds of returning children, and in 54:1 is told: "Sing for joy, you barren one who has borne no child!" Isaiah links her with Sarah (51:2). Paul quotes 54:1 for the 'Jerusalem above', the mother of believers (Galatians 4:27). The image reverses Babylon's fate in 47:8–9, where the proud queen loses husband and children in one day, and it recalls Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:5).

sections.h: Sarah, the mother of the people (Isaiah 51:2)
sections.b: Isaiah 51:2 is the only place outside Genesis where the Hebrew Bible names Sarah. The exiles are to look to Abraham, 'the rock', and Sarah, 'the quarry', from which they were cut (51:1): one childless couple became a nation. The barren wife of 54:1 continues the picture, and Paul reads Sarah as the free mother of the promise (Galatians 4:22–31).

"He was one man alone when I called him; / I blessed him, and I multiplied him" (51:2). Isaiah uses Abraham to encourage a small remnant: God made one man into many and can do so again. Ezekiel 33:24 records the same argument used presumptuously by those left in the land, and John the Baptist warns against trusting descent from Abraham (Matthew 3:9).

Isaiah 45–46 repeats again and again that the LORD alone is God: "I am the LORD, and there is no one else" (45:5, 6, 18, 21–22; 46:9). Babylon's boast "I am, and besides me there is nothing" (47:8, 10) is blasphemy for that reason. Paul gives the oath of 45:23, sworn by the one God, to Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11). Scholars often call these chapters the clearest statement of monotheism in the Hebrew Bible: the other gods are not rivals but nothing.

Isaiah's sharpest idol satire: Bel and Nebo are loaded on tired animals (46:1–2); worshipers buy gold, hire a smith and bow to the result, which must be carried and set in place and cannot answer (46:6–7). Against them stands the God who carries his people from birth to old age (46:3–4). The contrast turns on one verb: idols are a load that must be carried; the LORD is the one who carries. The idols' makers also fail the test of prophecy (46:9–11).

sections.h: The word that does not return empty (Isaiah 55:10–11)
sections.b: Chapters 40–55 begin with "our God's word will stand forever" (40:8) and end with the word that, like rain, "will not come back to me empty, / but it will do what I want" (55:11). The servant's mouth is a sharp sword (49:2), God sets his words in his people's mouth (51:16), and Zion's children will be "the LORD's learners" (54:13; John 6:45).

Isaiah 55:3 offers 'an everlasting covenant: the sure loyal love of David' to the whole people, at a time when no king of David's line ruled. Many scholars see the promise to David passed to the people (Westermann); others see a renewed Davidic ruler. Paul quotes the Greek in Acts 13:34 for the resurrection of Jesus, raised never to die again.

Isaiah 47 mocks Babylon's 'many sorceries' and 'spells' (47:9, 12), its charms against disaster (47:11), and 'the ones who map out the sky, / who stare at the stars, / who announce at every new moon' (47:13). Babylon had the ancient world's greatest tradition of omens and astronomy; the prophet says it could not foresee or avert its own fall.

sections.h: "Turn to me, all you ends of the earth" (Isaiah 45:14–25; 49:6; 52:15)
sections.b: The nations come to Zion confessing "Surely God is among you" (45:14) and are invited: "Turn to me, all you ends of the earth, and be saved" (45:22). The servant is "a light to the nations" (49:6), whose exaltation silences kings (52:15). The Greek of 54:15 even promises that 'proselytes will come to you'. Paul uses 52:15 to explain his mission to people who had never heard of Christ (Romans 15:21), and Acts 13:47 quotes 49:6 as the apostles' commission.

Jerusalem lies drunk in the streets from the cup of God's anger (51:17–20) and says, "The LORD has forgotten me" (49:14). God answers: "I have carved you on the palms of my hands" (49:16), takes the cup from her (51:22) and tells her to shake off the dust and sit enthroned (52:2). Her children are 'hurrying home' (49:17) in such numbers that the ruined city will be too small for them (49:19–20), and kings and queens will carry them (49:22–23).

A messenger crosses the mountains toward Zion with the news "Your God is King!" (52:7); the lookouts see the LORD returning to Zion (52:8), and the ruins of Jerusalem burst into song. Paul quotes 52:7 for the preachers of the gospel (Romans 10:15). The scene is the LORD's return as king to his city, a reversal of Ezekiel's vision of God's glory leaving the Temple (Ezekiel 10–11). The Targum renders the cry 'the kingdom of your God is revealed', and 11QMelchizedek applies the verse to the end time.

sections.h: God the husband who never divorced (Isaiah 50:1; 54:4–8)
sections.b: God asks for the divorce certificate he gave mother Zion (50:1): there is none. In 54:5–8 he calls himself her husband and Maker, who left her "for a little moment" and takes her back with "a loyal love that never ends". The image continues Hosea 2, Jeremiah 3 and Ezekiel 16. The certificate of divorce in Deuteronomy 24:1 ended a marriage for good; by denying that one was ever written, God makes Zion's return possible.

The servant goes silently "like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter, / like a ewe that falls silent in front of her shearers" (53:7). The Ethiopian official reads the verse in Acts 8:32, and the images of the Lamb of God (John 1:29) and the slaughtered Lamb (Revelation 5:6) draw on it, together with the Passover lamb. Jeremiah uses the same image of himself (Jeremiah 11:19).

Isaiah 53 is the Bible's fullest statement that one may suffer for the sins of others: "he was pierced for our rebellions" (53:5). The onlookers first assume the sufferer is being punished for his own sins (53:4), the reasoning of Job's friends. The Talmud reads 53:10 as the 'sufferings of love' that God sends to those he delights in (Berakhot 5a).

In Isaiah 40–55 righteousness is often God's saving action and the vindication of his people (45:8, 24–25; 54:17). The servant trusts that "the one who declares me in the right" is near (50:8), and himself 'will make the many righteous' and carry their guilt (53:11). Paul's language of justification draws on these chapters (Romans 4:25; 5:19; 8:33–34). The Greek of 45:25 says 'by the Lord they will be justified', with the verb Paul uses for justification.

sections.h: "Your God is King" and the kingdom revealed (Isaiah 52:7)
sections.b: The messenger's cry "Your God is King!" (52:7) uses the verb of the psalms' acclamation "The LORD is King!" (Psalm 93:1). The Targum renders it 'the kingdom of your God is revealed', close to Jesus's announcement that the kingdom of God has come near (Mark 1:14–15). Many scholars think that 52:7, with 40:9 and 61:1, explains why the Gospels pair 'good news' with 'the kingdom'. The returning king is the LORD himself, coming back to Zion as its lookouts watch (52:8).

God promises afflicted Zion foundations of lapis lazuli, battlements of rubies and gates of sparkling stones (54:11–12). Tobit 13:16–17 and Revelation 21:18–21 build their visions of the new Jerusalem from these verses, and a Qumran commentary (4Q164) reads the stones as the community's leaders. The Hebrew names of some stones are rare and uncertain, but the picture is clear: a city more splendid than the one destroyed, its children 'taught by the LORD' (54:13).

sections.h: "Look for the LORD while he lets himself be found" (Isaiah 55:6–7)
sections.b: The call to seek the LORD while he is near (55:6) is joined to the promise that he 'forgives over and over' (55:7). In the synagogue 55:6–56:8 is read on the afternoon of public fast days, and the Talmud applies 'while he is near' to the ten days of repentance before the Day of Atonement (Rosh Hashanah 18a). The verses that follow ground the invitation in God's mercy: his thoughts are higher than human thoughts, as the heavens are above the earth (55:8–9).

Isaiah 40–55 calls God Israel's go'el, 'redeemer', again and again (47:4; 48:17; 49:7, 26; 54:5, 8). Unlike a human redeemer, he pays no price: "For nothing you were sold, / and not with silver will you be bought back" (52:3), and Cyrus frees the exiles "not for a price" (45:13). The verb gaal is joined with 'buying back' (52:3, 9), and the redeemed return to Zion singing (51:10–11).
